20	CASE OD2-DEV2-SEQ: Hollin Vale Bank: small-business loan approvals nearly double
21	
22	Setting: Hollin Vale Bank is a fictional regional lender with 19 branches across the Maddern Valley. Branch loan officers take in small-business (SME) loan applications and collect the documents. All SME credit decisions are made centrally by the Credit Hub in Kestwick. In the second quarter the bank moved to a new loan-origination system (Corvane Origination), renewed its contract with its only valuation panel firm, refreshed its credit policy, and replaced five departing SME loan officers.
23	
24	Presenting request: The COO wants to know why SME loan approvals have taken longer since the spring and what the bank should do. Her month-end decision paper covers the Corvane contract and the performance of the new hires.
25	
26	INITIAL EVIDENCE
27	E1 [stage S1] Email from Imogen Raye, COO, to the executive team, 1 September (leadership-account): Subject: SME approvals. Since we switched to Corvane in April, our small-business approval times have nearly doubled: 13 days in August against 7 in March. On top of that we lost five experienced loan officers in Q2, and the replacements are still learning. By month-end I want two things. First, a decision paper on whether we withhold Corvane's final milestone payment and go back to the legacy workflow. Second, a plan from HR, with targets, to get the new hires up to speed. Customers are noticing, and withdrawals are up too.
28	E2 [stage S1] Monthly lending dashboard, SME loans, March–August (system-record): Median business days from application to decision, Mar–Aug: 7.2, 8.0, 9.6, 11.8, 13.1, 13.4. Applications received: 212, 205, 219, 224, 231, 228. Withdrawn before decision: 6.1%, 6.4%, 7.0%, 8.2%, 8.9%, 8.5%. Consumer loans (same branches, on Corvane since April), median days: 3.9, 4.6, 4.2, 4.0, 4.1, 4.0. The SME median rose at 18 of 19 branches. Footnote: since the Corvane cutover (14 April), SME applications with no customer document upload for 30 calendar days are auto-closed and counted as withdrawn. The legacy system left such files open indefinitely.
29	E3 [stage S1] HR summary for the COO, 22 August (document): SME loan officers: 34 at 1 April. Leavers April–June: 5 (3 retirements, 2 resignations to a competitor), average tenure 14 years. Replacements started between 6 May and 17 June at Ashby North, Brenmoor, Calder Quay, Hythe Lane and Overstrand. Two are internal transfers from consumer lending. All five completed the three-week Corvane and credit-procedures induction. Headcount was back to 34 by 17 June. Branch lending authorities are unchanged: the Credit Hub still makes all SME credit decisions centrally.
30	E4 [stage S1] Interview notes, Dev Okafor, Brenmoor branch manager, 26 August (manager-account): 'Corvane was painful in April. We were scanning everything twice and logins kept dropping. That's mostly settled now. The real problem starts once a file goes to the Hub. The status just says "With Credit Hub", it sits there a week or more, and then it comes back approved. Nobody tells us what they're doing. My new officer is fine on paperwork; on the system she's quicker than the man she replaced.' Asked whether all SME files are affected equally: 'Feels like it, but I haven't checked.'
31	E5 [stage S1] Operations change calendar, Q2 (extract) (change-record): 1 Apr – Valuation panel contract renewed with Pellow & Strand Valuers (sole panel firm). New fee schedule; service levels unchanged. 14 Apr – Corvane Origination goes live at all branches for consumer and SME lending. 1 May – Credit Policy v14 takes effect (annual refresh). Credit Policy Unit note: 'Largely editorial; no change to approval authorities or pricing.' 6 May–17 Jun – five replacement SME loan officers start (see HR summary). 3 Jun – one Credit Hub SME underwriter goes on parental leave; a contractor covers until November.

input.brief:
The slowdown is mostly in one place. The cause is not the Corvane system, the new hires or the valuation firm. It is the May credit policy refresh. Clause 6.3 lowered the threshold for a mandatory full property appraisal from $500k to $150k, and no one assessed its effect on processing time. Full appraisals took about 8.6 days at the valuer, against about 1.2 for desktop valuations. Full appraisals rose from about 30 a month to about 80. The median valuation stage for property-secured loans went from 1.7 days in April to 7.6 in June and 8.4 in August. Unsecured loans, which the policy change doesn't touch, are back to about 5.9 days. Underwriting time is flat. Document collection at the new hires' branches matches the other branches. The valuer's turnaround is unchanged, and valuation stage times were unchanged in April, after its contract renewed. Corvane caused a short April bump that has since cleared.

Recommendation: don't withhold Corvane's payment or revert to the legacy workflow. Don't put the new hires on improvement plans. Take the measured delay and the audit rationale (desktop valuations ran 12% above full appraisals) to the credit risk committee, and let it decide on the $150k threshold. Add a by-stage breakdown to the dashboard.

Withdrawals are uncertain. Part of the rise comes from the new 30-day auto-close rule, which the legacy system didn't have. Some customers did go elsewhere. I'd hold off on a fee rebate until that's sorted out.
